title: The Funeral Will Say Wonderful Things About You. Jesus’ Question Goes Deeper Than Your Reputation.
paragraphs: The Funeral Will Say Wonderful Things About You. Jesus’ Question Goes Deeper Than Your Reputation.

One day people may stand beside your coffin and speak beautifully about the life you lived. But there is one verdict no obituary, reputation, church résumé, or room full of mourners can give you: whether you truly belonged to Jesus Christ.
Your funeral will probably be kind to you.
Someone will stand behind a microphone with trembling hands and tell stories about your life.
They will remember your laughter.
They will talk about the people you helped.
Someone may say you were a wonderful father, mother, husband, wife, brother, sister, neighbor, coworker, pastor, ministry volunteer, or friend.
They may remember how generous you were.
How hard you worked.
How deeply you loved your family.
If you spent years around church, someone may mention your faith.
They may remember the Bible verses you posted.
The worship songs you loved.
The Sundays you attended.
The prayers you prayed.
The ministries you supported.
The people you encouraged.
And somewhere in that room, somebody may say the words almost every grieving heart desperately wants to believe:
“He’s with the Lord now.”
“She’s home.”
And perhaps they will be right.
God willing, gloriously right.
But here is the question that stopped me when I read the words of Jesus again:
What if everyone at your funeral has wonderful things to say about you... but the only verdict that ultimately matters is Christ’s?
That question is uncomfortable because reputation is something human beings can manage.
Reality before God is not.
We can polish a reputation.
We can learn Christian vocabulary.
We can know when to say “Amen.”
We can post Scripture while secretly starving spiritually.
We can learn how Christians talk before we ever learn what surrender feels like.
We can become familiar with Jesus without actually belonging to Jesus.
And that is why some of the most sobering words in the entire New Testament were not originally spoken to atheists mocking Christ.
Jesus said:
“Οὐ πᾶς ὁ λέγων μοι· Κύριε κύριε...”
Ou pas ho legōn moi, Kyrie Kyrie...
“Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord’...”
Notice those words.
Κύριε κύριε — Kyrie, Kyrie.
“Lord, Lord.”
These are people using the right title.
They know His name.
They address Jesus as Lord.
They are not standing there saying, “Jesus never existed.”
They are not laughing at Christianity.
They are appealing to Christ using language that sounds deeply religious.
And Jesus continues by describing people who point to extraordinary things they claim to have done in His name.
They effectively say:
Didn’t we prophesy in Your name?
Didn’t we cast out demons in Your name?
Didn’t we perform mighty works in Your name?
Listen carefully to what they are doing.
They are presenting their résumé.
Their defense is built around what they did.
We prophesied.
We cast out.
We performed.
We accomplished.
We had experiences.
We had ministry.
We had spiritual activity.
We had a reputation.
Surely that means we belonged to You.
Then comes the sentence that should make every person who casually wears the name “Christian” examine his or her heart.
Jesus says:
“οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς.”
Oudepote egnōn hymas.
“I never knew you.”
Not merely:
“You weren't impressive enough.”
Not:
“You didn't accomplish enough.”
Not:
“You had too many failures.”
The terrifying center of the statement is relational.
I never knew you.
And that distinction matters enormously, because this passage must never be twisted into the idea that salvation belongs to Christians who perform well enough.
That would contradict the Gospel itself.
We are not saved because our spiritual résumé impresses God.
We are saved by grace through faith. Salvation is God’s gift, not something we can boast about earning through works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
The same passage immediately continues by saying that those who are created in Christ Jesus are created for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
Grace saves.
And saving grace changes people.
Not into flawless people overnight.
Not into people who never struggle.
Not into people who never stumble.
But into people whose relationship to Christ, sin, repentance, obedience, and grace is being transformed.
That is why Matthew 7 should not drive a sincere, struggling believer into endless panic every time he falls.
Peter failed catastrophically.
He denied Jesus.
Three times.
Yet Peter’s failure was not the final chapter of Peter’s story.
Jesus restored him.
David sinned terribly.
The thief beside Christ reached the final hours of a ruined life with nothing resembling an impressive religious résumé.
Yet he turned toward Jesus, and Christ gave him hope beyond the grave.
The Gospel has never been the announcement that respectable people can save themselves.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
So Matthew 7 is not telling broken people, “Become perfect enough and maybe Jesus will accept you.”
It is confronting something far more deceptive.
A person can possess Christian familiarity without possessing Christ.
That is the danger.
You can know worship songs and not know the One being worshiped.
You can own several Bibles while rarely allowing Scripture to confront you.
You can defend Christianity online while refusing Christ access to the hidden rooms of your life.
You can know theology.
You can serve.
You can give.
You can preach.
You can build a following.
You can have “Christian” written across your biography.
And still there remains a question nobody else can answer for you:
Do you actually know Jesus Christ?
Not merely:
Do people think you are a Christian?
Not:
Were you baptized once?
Not:
Did your parents raise you in church?
Not:
Can you explain salvation?
Not:
Did you once repeat a prayer?
Not:
Do you have Christian friends?
Not:
But:
Have you entrusted yourself to Christ?
Have you come to Him as a sinner who cannot rescue himself?
Have you stopped negotiating with the sins you secretly intend to keep?
When you fall, do you run away from Christ to protect your darkness, or do you come back into His light in repentance?
Is Jesus merely part of your identity...
or is He your Lord?
Because there is a difference between struggling against sin and peacefully making a home inside it.
There is a difference between stumbling and surrendering to rebellion.
There is a difference between weakness that drives you toward Christ and lawlessness that continually tells Christ, in practice, “You may have my religious language, but You will not have my life.”
Matthew uses the Greek word ἀνομία — anomia in verse 23.
It carries the sense of lawlessness.
Jesus describes these people as workers of lawlessness.
Again, the contrast is not between “people who have never sinned” and “people who have sinned.”
If sinless performance were the requirement, none of us could stand.
The contrast forces us toward a deeper question:
Who actually rules the heart?
And suddenly the funeral feels closer.
Not because you are supposed to live terrified that you might die tonight.
Not because manufactured fear produces genuine conversion.
But because mortality strips away our illusions.
One day, your phone will stop receiving your messages.
Someone else will eventually clean out your drawers.
Your social-media account will become strangely quiet.
Pictures of you will remain after you are gone.
People may scroll backward through years of your life.
Someone will discover an old voice message and cry because hearing your voice suddenly hurts.
Your clothes will still exist.
Your chair may still sit where you left it.
Your Bible may still be on the shelf.
But you will have stepped beyond reputation.
And no amount of applause from this side of eternity will rewrite reality on the other.
That is why this is not really an article about funerals.
It is about today.
Because today you can still respond.
Today grace is still being proclaimed.
Today Christ is still calling sinners to Himself.
Today you can stop hiding behind the version of yourself everyone else knows.
Maybe nobody knows what happened last night.
Maybe nobody knows what you keep deleting from your phone.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your parents do not know.
Your children do not know.
Your followers certainly do not know.
Maybe everyone thinks you are doing wonderfully.
And inside, something is dying.
Maybe you have become skilled at looking spiritually alive.
You raise your hands during worship while carrying a secret you refuse to surrender.
You share sermons you are no longer living.
You encourage everyone else while privately wondering when you became so numb.
You know exactly how to sound strong.
“God is good.”
“I'm blessed.”
“Keep praying.”
“Trust His timing.”
Beautiful truths.
But when the room becomes quiet...
when nobody is watching...
when there is nothing left to perform...
you know there is distance between the person people applaud and the person God sees.
If that is you, please understand something.
Jesus did not expose hypocrisy so hypocrites would have no hope. He exposes darkness because He calls people into the light.
The One warning us in Matthew 7 is the same Jesus who goes toward the cross.
The hands that warn sinners will soon be pierced for sinners.
The voice saying that religious performance cannot save you belongs to the Savior who came precisely because you cannot save yourself.
That changes everything.
Christianity is not:
“Build a reputation impressive enough for heaven.”
It is:
Christ came to rescue sinners.
He lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is proclaimed in His name.
Your darkest chapter does not need to become the title of your eternity.
Your scandal does not have to be the last sentence.
Your pornography does not have to own you.
Your adultery does not have to define your final identity.
Your bitterness does not have to become your permanent home.
Your pride does not have to have the last word.
Your secret addiction does not outrank the mercy of Christ.
Your religious hypocrisy is not beyond His power to expose, forgive, cleanse, and transform.
But grace is not permission to keep hugging the chains Jesus died to break.
Grace calls you out.
Grace calls you home.
Grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
Grace does not merely change where forgiven sinners are going.
Grace begins changing the forgiven sinner.
This is where the theme of our lives becomes more than a slogan:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by telling you sin does not matter.

Jesus rewrites everything by meeting guilty people with truth and mercy, paying the price we could never pay, forgiving those who come to Him, and beginning a work of transformation that reaches deeper than reputation ever could.
Maybe your scandal isn't public.
Maybe your scandal lives entirely inside you.
Nobody knows.
But Jesus knows.
And somehow that is both terrifying and beautiful.
Because the Person who knows the worst thing about you is the very One inviting you to stop hiding.
You do not need to impress Him.
You cannot manipulate Him.
You cannot edit the footage.
You cannot delete the history.
You cannot hand Jesus the carefully curated version of yourself you hand everybody else.
He already knows.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you become more respectable.
Not after you fix yourself.
Come as the sinner who finally admits:
“Jesus, I need You.”
Maybe you have called Him “Lord” for twenty years.
Then ask yourself something deeper tonight.
Does my life reveal that I want Jesus Himself, or merely the benefits associated with His name?
Do I love Christ?
Do I trust Christ?
When Scripture confronts me, am I willing to be corrected?
When I sin, do I excuse it indefinitely, or does the Spirit draw me toward confession and repentance?
Do I want Jesus to save me only from hell, or do I also want Him to save me from the sin destroying me?
And please do not turn those questions into another performance checklist.
The answer is not to stare endlessly at yourself until you manufacture assurance.
Look to Christ.
The Christian's confidence ultimately rests not in the perfection of his grip upon Jesus but in the sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
Come to Him.
Trust Him.
Remain in Him.
Follow Him.
When you fall, confess.
When you wander, return.
When sin whispers that hiding would be easier, drag the darkness into the light.
When shame tells you that Jesus is finished with you, remember the cross.
When pride tells you that you don't need mercy, remember the cross again.
At the cross, both despair and arrogance lose their arguments.
You are more sinful than your reputation admits.
And Christ is more merciful than your shame wants you to believe.
Imagine your funeral again.
People are standing there.
They tell wonderful stories.
They speak your name with affection.
Perhaps they say you were successful.
Generous.
Funny.
Faithful.
Strong.
Perhaps hundreds of people comment beneath your final photograph.
But imagine something better than being remembered well.
Imagine actually belonging to Christ.
Imagine your deepest confidence at the end of life not being:
“People thought I was good.”
But:
“My hope is Jesus Christ.”
Not my résumé.
Not my reputation.
Not my ministry.
Not my followers.
Not my charitable acts.
Not my denomination.
Not my family history.
Not my public image.
Christ.
Only Christ.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose.
The One who receives those who come to Him.
The One whose grace can take the chapters we thought had ruined everything and begin writing redemption where we expected only shame.
And maybe that is why you needed to read this before your funeral instead of having someone read something beautiful about you at it.
You still have breath.
There is still time to be honest.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to tell strangers every private detail. But you can stop pretending before God.
If you need words, let them be simple:
“Jesus, have mercy on me. I have hidden behind appearances long enough. I cannot save myself. Forgive me. Cleanse me. I trust You. Teach me to follow You—not merely with my mouth, but with my life.”
Not because typing three words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes honesty begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Then think of one person you love.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to condemn.
Someone you genuinely love.
Someone who knows Christianity but may not truly know Christ.
Someone who has been running.
Someone who thinks being respectable is enough.
Someone whose wounds have driven them away from church.
Someone who believes their scandal has permanently disqualified them from grace.
Or send this privately.
Read Matthew 7 again when the noise disappears.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront what needs confronting, heal where Christ is healing you, and grow deeper in Jesus, follow and stay connected.
Supporting Gospel ministry does not purchase God's favor, prove that you love Him, or earn salvation. We never want to manipulate something as sacred as glorifying God into a financial transaction.
But one genuine way believers may choose to glorify God is by willingly using their resources, reach, and influence to help sound Gospel teaching reach others.
Come to Jesus.
Because someday the room may be filled with people saying wonderful things about you.
Let them.
Love them well enough that they have wonderful things to remember.
Live humbly.
Serve generously.
Repent quickly.
Forgive freely.
Love deeply.
But never confuse their applause with Christ's salvation.
Your obituary cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot know Jesus for you.
Your pastor cannot surrender for you.
Your parents' faith cannot substitute for yours.
Your ministry cannot become your mediator.
There is one Mediator between God and humanity: Jesus Christ.
So before people gather someday to talk about how well they knew you, settle the infinitely greater question:
Do you belong to the Christ whose name you know?
And if that question unsettles you tonight, don't bury it beneath another distraction.
Open the Gospel.
Pray.
Seek Christ.
Talk with a mature, biblically faithful believer.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
There may come a day when people speak your name for the final time.
But the greatest story of your life will never be what people said about you after you died.
It will be what Jesus Christ did with a sinner who finally stopped hiding and came home.
Your funeral may remember the person everyone thought you were. Grace is rewriting the person Jesus already knows.
